## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read

- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. 6	The role of a short post-lunch nap in improving cognitive, motor,
7	and sprint performance in participants with partial sleep deprivation
8	
9	
10	J. WATERHOUSE, G. ATKINSON, B. EDWARDS, & T. REILLY
11	
12	Research Institute for Sport and Exercise Sciences, Liverpool John Moores University, Liverpool, UK
13	
14	(Accepted 26 January 2007)
15	
16	
17	
18	Abstract
19	The aim of this study was to determine the effects of a post-lunch nap on subjective alertness and performance following
20	partial sleep loss. Ten healthy males (mean age 23.3 years, s ¼ 3.4) either napped or sat quietly from 13:00 to 13:30 h after a
21	night of shortened sleep (sleep 23:00 – 03:00 h only). Thirty minutes after the afternoon nap or control (no-nap) condition,
22	alertness, short-term memory, intra-aural temperature, heart rate, choice reaction time, grip strength, and times for 2-m and
23	20-m sprints were recorded. The afternoon nap lowered heart rate and intra-aural temperature. Alertness, sleepiness, short-
24	term memory, and accuracy at the 8-choice reaction time test were improved by napping (P 5 0.05), but mean reaction
25	times and grip strength were not affected (P 4 0.05). Sprint times were improved. Mean time for the 2-m sprints fell from
26	1.060 s (sx ¼ 0.018) to 1.019 s (sx ¼ 0.019) (P ¼ 0.031 paired t-test); mean time for the 20-m sprints fell from 3.971 s
27	(sx ¼ 0.054) to 3.878 s (sx ¼ 0.047) (P ¼ 0.013). These results indicate that a post-lunch nap improves alertness and aspects
28	of mental and physical performance following partial sleep loss, and have implications for athletes with restricted sleep during
29	training or before competition.

Journal of Sports Sciences, December 2007; 25(14): 1557 – 1566




The role of a short post-lunch nap in improving cognitive, motor,
and sprint performance in participants with partial sleep deprivation


J. WATERHOUSE, G. ATKINSON, B. EDWARDS, & T. REILLY

Research Institute for Sport and Exercise Sciences, Liverpool John Moores University, Liverpool, UK

(Accepted 26 January 2007)



Abstract
The aim of this study was to determine the effects of a post-lunch nap on subjective alertness and performance following
partial sleep loss. Ten healthy males (mean age 23.3 years, s ¼ 3.4) either napped or sat quietly from 13:00 to 13:30 h after a
night of shortened sleep (sleep 23:00 – 03:00 h only). Thirty minutes after the afternoon nap or control (no-nap) condition,
alertness, short-term memory, intra-aural temperature, heart rate, choice reaction time, grip strength, and times for 2-m and
20-m sprints were recorded. The afternoon nap lowered heart rate and intra-aural temperature. Alertness, sleepiness, short-
term memory, and accuracy at the 8-choice reaction time test were improved by napping (P 5 0.05), but mean reaction
times and grip strength were not affected (P 4 0.05). Sprint times were improved. Mean time for the 2-m sprints fell from
1.060 s (sx ¼ 0.018) to 1.019 s (sx ¼ 0.019) (P ¼ 0.031 paired t-test); mean time for the 20-m sprints fell from 3.971 s
(sx ¼ 0.054) to 3.878 s (sx ¼ 0.047) (P ¼ 0.013). These results indicate that a post-lunch nap improves alertness and aspects
of mental and physical performance following partial sleep loss, and have implications for athletes with restricted sleep during
training or before competition.

Keywords: Sleep loss, athletic performance, fatigue, daytime sleep

113	 INTRODUCTION
114	
115	       The ability to generate force and power through the lower extremities during athletic
116	
117	tasks such as jumping is a critical determinant of performance (1–3). The countermovement
118	
119	jump (CMJ) is a foundational movement for various sport-specific skills and is widely used by
120	
121	sports medicine and science practitioners as a time-efficient testing method for assessing lower-
122	
123	body power, performance, and readiness for return to play from injury (4–6).
124	
125	                                                                D
126	       Larger muscle size is known to relate to greater force and power production (7, 8).
127	
128	However, traditional imaging methods for quantifying muscle volumes to assess function are
129	
130	
131	
132	                                            TE
133	time-intensive, requiring manual segmentation and extensive processing, limiting the scope of
134	
135	investigations to key muscle groups and smaller sample sizes. As a result, prior research
136	
137	examining the relationship between muscle size and jump performance has primarily focused on
138	
139	
140	
141	
142	                      EP
143	a select few muscles, particularly the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, and lateral gastrocnemius as
144	
145	predictors of jump performance (8–10). Further, most studies have strictly investigated the
146	
147	muscle morphology (e.g. anatomical cross-sectional area or thickness) and architecture (e.g.,
148	
149	pennation angle, fascicle length, and physiological cross-sectional area) of large, primary
150	
151	           C
152	muscles, but less is known about the role of other muscles (2, 8, 11). Traditional approaches to
153	
154	imaging may overlook contributions from other lower extremity muscles and limit our
155	
156	C
157	understanding of how these muscles influence jump performance.
158	
159	       Advancements in machine learning technology have enabled the rapid measurement of
160	
161	A
162	muscle volumes from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, offering the opportunity to
163	
164	quantify various lower extremity muscle volumes. This technology has demonstrated utility in
165	
166	assessing associations between muscle volume and sprint and vertical jump performance in male
167	
168	basketball players and untrained individuals, as well as persistent muscle atrophy post-surgery

484	       Quadricep muscles facilitate extension of the knee, providing the primary vertical
485	
486	propulsion for the lower extremities during jumping (8, 18). Prior studies assessing a select
487	
488	number of lower extremity muscles have shown relationships between quadriceps strength and
489	
490	thickness and jump performance (10, 19). In our analysis, vastus lateralis was strongly associated
491	
492	with both jump height and peak power when included amongst an expanded pool of lower
493

495	extremity muscles. The vastus lateralis was highly correlated with the vastus medialis and vastus
496	
497	intermedius volumes (Supplemental Table 4, Supplemental Digital Content,
498

502	http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362), suggesting it may be representative of overall quadriceps
503	
504	muscle volume. In addition, the vastus lateralis is the largest of the quadriceps muscles, making
505	
506	it particularly influential in vertical propulsion during jumping (20, 21). Given these findings,
507

The Role of Lower-Limb Muscle Volumes in Vertical Jump Performance in NCAA

Division 1 Athletes

Dan O’Brien, Naoaki Ito, Stephanie Kliethermes, and Bryan Heiderscheit

Department of Orthopedics and Rehabilitation, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI

Running Title: MUSCLE VOLUMES AND VERTICAL JUMP PERFORMANCE
                                                               D
Address for correspondence: Bryan Heiderscheit, 1685 Highland Ave, Madison, WI 53706;



                                           TE
Phone: (608) 263-5428; E-mail: heiderscheit@wisc.edu

Conflict of Interest and Funding Source: This work was supported by the University of

Wisconsin Department of Orthopedics and Rehabilitation Freedom of Movement and Pilot




                      EP
Award programs and the National Football League (NFL). The authors would like to

acknowledge the Sports Medicine staff in the University of Wisconsin-Madison Division of

Athletics for their commitment to the welfare of the student-athletes and contributions to the

Badger Athletic Performance program. Bryan Heiderscheit is an advisory board member for

          C
Springbok Analytics (stock options). Stephanie Kliethermes is a statistical consultant for

Springbok Analytics. The remaining authors declare that they have no competing interests.

C
A
                                                1



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 ABSTRACT

Introduction/Purpose: This study examined the relationship between lower extremity muscle

volumes and countermovement jump (CMJ) performance in 207 (43 female, 164 male) NCAA

Division I collegiate basketball, football, hockey, and soccer athletes. The primary aim was to

determine which combination of lower extremity muscle volumes was most strongly associated

with CMJ performance across a large subset of high-level college athletes. Methods: Athletes

                                                                D
underwent bilateral MRI scans, and muscle volumes were quantified using machine-learning-

based auto-segmentation. CMJ height (cm) and peak power (W/kg) were measured using dual



                                            TE
force plates. Backward selection regression analyses determined muscle combinations that best

explained variance in jump performance after adjusting for sex and sport. Results: Vastus

lateralis muscle volume was related to both jump height (β = 0.36, p < 0.01) and peak power (β =




                      EP
0.41, p < 0.01). In addition to the vastus lateralis, the jump height model retained rectus femoris,

and the peak power model retained soleus, gluteus medius, adductor magnus, and biceps femoris

long head. The differing muscle candidates in the two models likely reflect the distinct features

of each CMJ metric: jump height reflects force over time (impulse, N·s) while peak power

           C
reflects the rapid generation of force (N·m/s). Sport-specific differences emerged, with hockey

and football athletes displaying greater jump heights and generating greater peak power when

C
compared to basketball players. Male athletes outperformed females in both jump metrics.

Conclusions: These findings, derived from over 200 NCAA Division I athletes, highlight the

A
crucial role of the quadriceps in CMJ performance in high-level athletes. Strength and

conditioning and rehabilitation programs may consider targeting quadriceps hypertrophy to

improve vertical jump performance. Key Words: COUNTERMOVEMENT JUMP,

MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING, VASTUS LATERALIS, QUADRICEPS


                                                 2



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 INTRODUCTION

       The ability to generate force and power through the lower extremities during athletic

tasks such as jumping is a critical determinant of performance (1–3). The countermovement

jump (CMJ) is a foundational movement for various sport-specific skills and is widely used by

sports medicine and science practitioners as a time-efficient testing method for assessing lower-

body power, performance, and readiness for return to play from injury (4–6).

                                                                D
       Larger muscle size is known to relate to greater force and power production (7, 8).

However, traditional imaging methods for quantifying muscle volumes to assess function are



                                            TE
time-intensive, requiring manual segmentation and extensive processing, limiting the scope of

investigations to key muscle groups and smaller sample sizes. As a result, prior research

examining the relationship between muscle size and jump performance has primarily focused on




                      EP
a select few muscles, particularly the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, and lateral gastrocnemius as

predictors of jump performance (8–10). Further, most studies have strictly investigated the

muscle morphology (e.g. anatomical cross-sectional area or thickness) and architecture (e.g.,

pennation angle, fascicle length, and physiological cross-sectional area) of large, primary

           C
muscles, but less is known about the role of other muscles (2, 8, 11). Traditional approaches to

imaging may overlook contributions from other lower extremity muscles and limit our

C
understanding of how these muscles influence jump performance.

       Advancements in machine learning technology have enabled the rapid measurement of

A
muscle volumes from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, offering the opportunity to

quantify various lower extremity muscle volumes. This technology has demonstrated utility in

assessing associations between muscle volume and sprint and vertical jump performance in male

basketball players and untrained individuals, as well as persistent muscle atrophy post-surgery


                                                 3



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 and in elite athlete populations (12, 13). This study aimed to determine which combination of

lower extremity muscle volumes was most strongly associated with CMJ performance across a

large subset of high-level college athletes.

METHODS

       This cross-sectional study included a cohort of National Collegiate Athletic Association

(NCAA) Division 1 American football, basketball, ice hockey, and soccer athletes from a single

                                                                 D
institution. Before their competitive season, athletes completed CMJ testing on force plates and

underwent bilateral lower extremity MRI scans. All athletes provided informed consent for the



                                               TE
use of their CMJ and MRI data as part of their respective parent studies, each of which was

approved by the University of Wisconsin–Madison Health Sciences IRB. Athletes were eligible

for inclusion if they were cleared to participate in sport activities without limitation in practice




                       EP
and games at the time of data collection and had both CMJ and MRI data available and collected

within four months of each other.

Jump Performance

       Athletes performed bilateral maximum effort CMJs on portable, dual force platforms that

           C
measured vertical forces at a sampling rate of 800 Hz, with the software’s internal filtering

applied (Leonardo Mechanograph; Novotec Medical, Pforzheim, Germany). Athletes started

C
with one foot on each force plate and hands placed on their hips. Athletes were instructed to

“jump as high as possible” while maintaining their hands on their hips throughout the jump. A

A
jump trial was considered successful if athletes landed with one foot on each force plate and

maintained their balance. Athletes completed up to three successful trials. If a trial was

unsuccessful, the athlete repeated the attempt, up to a maximum of five total jump trials per

testing session.


                                                  4



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 Quantifying Muscle Volume

       Athletes from all sports underwent MRI of the lumbopelvic region and bilateral lower

extremities using a 1.5T SIGNA Voyager Air Edition Mobile MRI (GE HealthCare, Chicago, IL,

USA) or a 3-T scanner (SIGNA Premier [GE Healthcare]) equipped with a flexible surface coil.

Imaging was performed continuously from the 12th thoracic vertebra to below the ankle joint in

sets of 40 scans to capture the entire field of view. Axial multislice 2-dimensional fast spoiled

                                                                D
gradient recalled echo (FSPGR) sequences were utilized, with parameters optimized to maximize

the muscle signal and minimize the fat signal (repetition time/echo time: 839 ms/4.35 ms; field



                                           TE
of view: 500 × 344 mm; matrix: 256 × 176; voxel size: 2 × 2 × 5 mm). In all instances, the

acquired images were processed using automated machine-learning-based auto-segmentation

algorithms to obtain 38 individual muscle volumes for each limb (Springbok Analytics,




                       EP
Charlottesville, VA), which has demonstrated repeatability comparable with interobserver

variability (14, 15). Muscle volumes were then normalized to athletes' body mass and height

(mL·kg⁻¹·cm⁻¹) (14).

Muscle and Jump Variable Selection

           C
       Jump height (cm) and peak power (W) were the primary variables of interest in the CMJ.

Peak power during the concentric takeoff phase was assessed (i.e., the period of upward

C
propulsion until foot-off), and jump height was calculated based on impulse momentum from the

proprietary Leonardo Mechanograph software. Data from the trial with the highest jump height

A
were extracted, and takeoff peak power from the same trial was normalized to body mass (W/kg)

to allow for comparison across athletes. Given that the joint movements responsible for the CMJ

primarily occur in the sagittal plane, we only included the 23 lower extremity muscles

responsible for flexion and extension at the hip, knee, and ankle as candidate variables for


                                                 5



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 analysis (Figure 1). Since the CMJ is a bilateral task, we summed the muscle volumes from both

sides to obtain a single volume for each muscle to use for analysis.

Statistical Analyses

          Descriptive statistics (mean ± standard deviation) were calculated for height, weight,

jump height (cm), normalized peak power (W/kg), and normalized muscle volumes

(mL·kg⁻¹·cm⁻¹). Multiple regression analyses with backwards selection were conducted to

                                                                 D
determine the combination of muscle volumes that best explained variance in jump height and

peak power. Both sex (male, female) and sport (basketball, football, hockey, soccer) were forced


                                             TE
into the model as potential covariates. The analysis began with a full model that included all 23

muscle volumes. The least contributing muscle was removed at each iteration based on the

Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), calculated to penalize additional candidate muscles and




                        EP
reduce overfitting. The process continued until no muscle removed from the model decreased the

Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) score by greater than two points (16). Effect estimates (β)

and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) are reported, as well as the unadjusted and adjusted R2

values.

             C
          Given the model findings, a post hoc F-test comparing nested linear models was run as a

separate analysis to test the significance of the interaction between biceps femoris long head and

C
vastus lateralis in the peak power model. Type III ANOVAs were performed on the final

regression models to assess the overall effect of sport. Multicollinearity was assessed using the

A
variance inflation factor (VIF) to identify candidate variables exceeding the threshold of five. All

statistical analyses were performed in R (Version 4.4.1; R Core Team 2024), with the following

packages: broom (v1.0.7), car (v3.1.2), corrplot (v0.92), dplyr (v1.1.4), ggcorrplot (v0.1.4.1),

ggplot2 (v3.5.1), lm.beta (v1.7.2), MASS (v7.3.60.2).


                                                   6



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 RESULTS

       Two hundred and seven collegiate athletes were included in the study (Supplemental

Table 1, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362), comprised of 164

males (height: 187.3 ± 7.6 cm, weight: 98.4 ± 20.0 kg) and 43 females (172.0 ± 8.1 cm, 69.5 ±

10.5 kg).

       Following backward selection, the final model for CMJ jump height (Fig. 2;

                                                               D
Supplemental Table 2, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362)

explained 54% of the variance in jump height (R² = 0.56, adjusted R² = 0.54). The model



                                           TE
included the vastus lateralis (estimate [95% CI] = 1.39 [0.91, 1.87], β = 0.36, p < 0.01) and

rectus femoris (1.20 [-0.11, 2.51], β = 0.11, p = 0.07) muscle volumes after adjusting for sex and

sport. A 1 mL·kg⁻¹·cm⁻¹ greater vastus lateralis muscle volume related to a 1.39 [0.91, 1.87] cm




                      EP
higher jump height. A Type III ANOVA indicated a significant main effect of sport (F(3, 200) =

7.68, p < .001). Marginal sport and sex specific regression coefficients were examined relative to

basketball (reference sport) and female (reference sex), and both are adjusted for all other

variables in the model. Hockey (6.63 [3.63, 9.63], β = 0.27, p < 0.01) and football (3.76 [1.26,

            C
6.26], β = 0.22, p < 0.01) were associated with higher jump heights, whereas no difference was

noted in soccer when compared to basketball players. On average, males also jumped higher than

C
females (8.86 [6.52, 11.20], β = 0.43, p < 0.01).

       The final model for peak power (Fig. 2; Supplemental Table 3, Supplemental Digital

A
Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362) explained 71% of the variance in peak power

(R² = 0.72, adjusted R² = 0.71). The model included vastus lateralis (1.67 [1.20, 2.14], β = 0.41,

p < .01), gluteus medius (1.16 [-0.04, 2.36], β = 0.11, p = 0.06), biceps femoris long head (-1.78,

[-3.36, -0.20], β = -0.11, p = 0.03), adductor magnus (0.66 [0.12, 1.20], β = 0.13, p = 0.02), and


                                                    7



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 soleus (1.54 [0.63, 2.44], β = 0.16, p < 0.01) muscle volumes after adjusting for sex and sport. A

1 mL·kg⁻¹·cm⁻¹ greater vastus lateralis muscle volume related to a 1.67 [1.20, 2.14] W/kg higher

peak power. A Type III ANOVA indicated a significant main effect of sport (F(3, 197) = 11.18,

p < .001). Specifically, football (4.49 [2.26, 6.72], p < .01) was associated with greater peak

power compared to basketball players, whereas hockey or soccer, compared to basketball, was

not statistically significant. Males also generated greater peak power than females (8.79 [6.75,

10.83], p < .01).
                                                                D
        Multicollinearity analysis revealed that all muscle volumes in the final models had VIF

values below the threshold of five.

DISCUSSION
                                           TE
        This study used a dataset of over 200 NCAA Division 1 college athletes to determine the




                      EP
relationship between lower extremity muscle volumes and CMJ performance. After accounting

for sex and sport, vastus lateralis muscle volume was identified to be a major contributor to both

jump height and peak power, underscoring its key role in vertical jump performance. In addition

to the vastus lateralis, which was the only muscle common to both regression models, the jump

           C
height model included the rectus femoris, while the peak power model retained the soleus,

gluteus medius, adductor magnus, and biceps femoris long head. The differing muscle candidates

C
in the two models likely reflect the distinct features of each CMJ metric: jump height reflects

force over time (impulse, N·s) while peak power reflects the rapid generation of force (N·m/s)

A
(17).




                                                 8



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 Importance of the Quadriceps in Jump Performance

       Quadricep muscles facilitate extension of the knee, providing the primary vertical

propulsion for the lower extremities during jumping (8, 18). Prior studies assessing a select

number of lower extremity muscles have shown relationships between quadriceps strength and

thickness and jump performance (10, 19). In our analysis, vastus lateralis was strongly associated

with both jump height and peak power when included amongst an expanded pool of lower

                                                                D
extremity muscles. The vastus lateralis was highly correlated with the vastus medialis and vastus

intermedius volumes (Supplemental Table 4, Supplemental Digital Content,



                                            TE
http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362), suggesting it may be representative of overall quadriceps

muscle volume. In addition, the vastus lateralis is the largest of the quadriceps muscles, making

it particularly influential in vertical propulsion during jumping (20, 21). Given these findings,




                       EP
targeting hypertrophy of the vastus lateralis, and by extension the quadriceps, may be a

promising strategy to enhance jump performance, although longitudinal studies are needed to

establish a causal relationship.

       Besides the vastus lateralis, both jump height and peak power regression models

           C
contained additional unique muscles, though their influences were less pronounced. In the jump

height model, the rectus femoris was the only other muscle retained. Given that it crosses both

C
the hip and knee and undergoes minimal length change during the CMJ, the rectus femoris may

primarily transfer energy between joints rather than significantly contribute to vertical propulsion

A
(22, 23). However, because it spans both joints, greater rectus femoris volume may allow for

more effective force transmission from the hip to the knee during push-off and help transfer

energy during rapid knee extension. Increased muscle volume may also reflect adaptations in

muscle architecture (e.g., greater physiological cross‑sectional area and stiffness) that enable the


                                                 9



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 rectus femoris to sustain and transmit higher forces and enhance inter‑joint energy transfer

during the CMJ. In the peak power model, soleus, gluteus medius, adductor magnus, and biceps

femoris long head were retained alongside the vastus lateralis. The soleus primarily contributes

to vertical ground reaction force through ankle plantarflexion and indirectly assists knee

extension through closed-chain mechanics, though it has less mechanical advantage at the knee

than the vastus lateralis in vertical jump (24, 25). Although the gluteus medius and adductor

                                                               D
magnus aid in hip extension, their activation patterns suggest their primary role may be

stabilizing the hip joint, thereby optimizing force transfer through the lower extremity during the

CMJ (25).
                                           TE
       Conversely, our findings showed that smaller biceps femoris long head muscle volume

was related to greater jump power. An interaction effect was observed between vastus lateralis




                      EP
and biceps femoris long head muscle volumes in our post hoc analysis (Supplemental Table 5,

Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362), demonstrating that a possible

trade-off between muscle volume distribution and peak jump power may exist. This finding

highlights the possibility that greater muscle size may not always be beneficial toward the task of

            C
interest, in this case the CMJ. As such, understanding how specific muscle size distributions

impact lower extremity biomechanics and power output provides deeper insights into optimizing

C
jump mechanics.

Sport Differences

A      On average, hockey players jumped the highest (Table 1), likely reflecting their sport-

specific demands, which require consistent, powerful hip and knee extension for skating strides

(26). Male hockey players also had notably larger normalized quadriceps volumes, particularly in

the vastus lateralis and vastus medialis, which may also explain their greater jump heights


                                                10



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 (Supplemental Table 6, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362).

Basketball players, despite frequently jumping during sport, demonstrated lower jump heights

compared to hockey, football, and soccer athletes. Our findings also indicated that athletes with

larger quadricep muscle volumes relative to body size generally produced greater peak power.

This relationship was most pronounced in male hockey players.

Limitations

                                                                D
       As this study involved high-level collegiate athletes at a single institution, the findings

may not be fully generalizable to recreational, high school, or professional populations. Second,



                                           TE
while our models identified muscle volumes significantly associated with CMJ performance,

these muscles may not contribute similarly to other movements required in each specific sport.

Third, given the cross-sectional study design, there is no direct evidence to support that training




                      EP
for hypertrophy in these identified muscle groups will result in better jump performance. Fourth,

because this was an exploratory analysis, it is important to note that our use of multiple

regression procedures (including backward selection and a post hoc interaction test) may have

increased the risk of type I error. Lastly, the measurement of muscle volume provides unique

           C
insights into characterizing individual muscle contribution to CMJ, but is not a direct measure of

muscle strength.

C
CONCLUSIONS

       We identified that quadriceps muscle volume, particularly the vastus lateralis, was most

A
strongly associated with CMJ height and peak power in elite athletes after accounting for sex and

sport. While other muscles, such as the gluteus medius, rectus femoris, biceps femoris long head,

adductor magnus, and soleus, were related to jump performance, their influence was less

pronounced. These findings highlight the critical role of the quadriceps in vertical jump


                                                 11



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 performance and suggest that strength and conditioning and rehabilitation programs may

consider targeting quadriceps hypertrophy to improve vertical jump performance.

the student-athletes and contributions to the Badger Athletic Performance program. Bryan

4	The role of genetic and                                                                 © The Author(s) 2025

15	Souad Kartti2,3, Elmostafa El Fahime2,3, Saber Boutayeb2,3,
16	Younes Chagar5, Christophe Baudot5, Lahcen Belyamani2,3,5,6,

21	Abstract
22	Understanding how genetic and epigenetic factors inﬂuence predisposition, susceptibility,
23	protection, severity, and recovery potential in sports-related muscle, bone, and brain injuries
24	is gaining increasing attention, as these injuries represent a major concern for athletes’
25	health and performance. This narrative review explores the role of speciﬁc genetic variants,
26	such as those in ACE, ACTN3, AMPD1, VDR, and APOE, in predisposing athletes to injury.
27	In parallel, the emerging role of microRNAs, including miR-21, miR-133a, miR-208a, and
28	miR-214 in regulating gene expression related to muscle regeneration, inﬂammation, and
29	neuroprotection, is highlighted. These small noncoding RNAs are inﬂuenced by environ-
30	mental stimuli such as sports activity and training, and may serve as promising biomarkers
31	
32

45	6

47	7

49	Morocco
50

52	Amina Marrouh, Laboratory of Drug Sciences, Mohammed VI Faculty of Pharmacy, Mohammed VI University
53	of Sciences and Health - UM6SS, Casablanca 20370, Morocco.
54	Email: amarrouh@um6ss.ma
55	
56	               Creative Commons Non Commercial CC BY-NC: This article is distributed under the terms

59	the work without further permission provided the original work is attributed as speciﬁed on the SAGE and
60	Open Access page (https://us.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/open-access-at-sage).
61	 2                                                                    Science Progress 108(4)
62	
63	
64	for injury risk and recovery. This review is based on a narrative approach, involving targeted
65	literature searches in databases such as PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, with no
66	restrictions on language or publication date. Articles were selected based on relevance using
67	predeﬁned keywords and were categorized by injury type (muscular, bone, and concussion-
68	related). However, several limitations remain, including population heterogeneity, small sam-
69	ple sizes, and the lack of functional validation of identiﬁed variants, which currently limits
70	their clinical application. Ethical considerations surrounding the use of genetic data in ath-
71	letes also need to be addressed. In the future, better integration of multiomic data could
72	support the development of personalized and ethically sound strategies for injury prevention
73	and athlete care.
74	
75	Keywords
76	Concussions, epigenetics, musculoskeletal injuries, SNP, sports genetics
77	
78	
79	Introduction
80	The predisposition to injury and sports performance is primarily determined by intrinsic
81	biological traits, including genetic polymorphisms that inﬂuence muscle structure, bone
82	density, and neuromuscular function. While training and other extrinsic factors can
83	modulate injury risk, they do not deﬁne the baseline predisposition, which is rooted in
84	these intrinsic characteristics.
85	    The Healthy Injury-Free Adolescent Athletes study has shown that multiple factors,
86	including biomechanical, environmental, and psychosocial aspects, contribute signiﬁ-
87	cantly to injury risk in young athletes.1 Similarly, studies on Olympic athletes have
88	demonstrated that elite-level performance tends to run in families, emphasizing the
89	important contribution of genetic background.2 Foundational studies further suggest
90	that up to 60–70% of the variability in physiological adaptations to physical activity
91	(such as VO2max and strength gains) and injury susceptibility may be explained by gen-
92	etic factors.3 Engaging in intense physical activity comes with an increased risk of injur-
93	ies, the nature and severity of which vary depending on the sport. Indeed, each sport has a
94	speciﬁc risk proﬁle, related to its unique physical and technical demands. Nearly 70% of
95	track and ﬁeld athletes experience injuries per season.4 Lower limb injuries are extremely
96	common in certain sports, affecting 50% of athletes participating in football, marathon,
97	triathlon, gymnastics (female), basketball, pole vaulting, rugby sevens, volleyball
98	(female), handball, and tennis.5 Among these injuries, muscular injuries such as ham-
99	string strains are particularly prevalent; for instance, professional footballers experience
100	a 20% hamstring injury rate per season, with 20% of these progressing to a chronic stage.6
101	Stress fractures and stress reactions, while less frequent, pose a greater challenge due to
102	their longer recovery periods, with athletes requiring on average 67.4 days (± 73.1) to
103	return to full training for stress reactions, and up to 199 days (± 205.2) for stress frac-
104	tures.7 In comparison, concussions, though less common, are a growing concern in con-
105	tact sports, with rugby union players experiencing concussion rates between 8.2 and
106	16.11 per 1000 h of activity, Gaelic football players 5.21 per 1000 h, and football players
107	 Marrouh et al.                                                                                  3
108	
109	
110	between 2.08 and 4.04 per 1000 activity events.8 Beyond the biological and environmen-
111	tal factors inﬂuencing predisposition and injury risk, it is important to consider the sig-
112	niﬁcant economic impact of sports injuries. A recent literature review revealed that,
113	despite methodological heterogeneity, studies consistently report substantial direct and
114	indirect costs associated with sports injuries, including medical expenses, income loss,
115	and reduced quality of life.9 For example, a study conducted in Switzerland analyzing
116	702 injuries in amateur football estimated an average cost of €4030 per injury, with costs
117	reaching up to €8190 for players over 30 competing in speciﬁc amateur leagues.10 These
118	ﬁgures illustrate the considerable burden sports injuries place on healthcare systems and
119	individuals, underscoring the urgent need for effective prevention and management strat-
120	egies tailored to the speciﬁc demands of each sport.
121	    Research has increasingly focused on the genetic basis of athletic status. For example,
122	a genome-wide linkage scan involving 700 pairs of British dizygotic twins estimated that
123	approximately 66% of the variance in athlete status could be explained by genetic factors,
124	according to the speciﬁc assumptions of the twin study design. This estimate, however,
125	varies across sport disciplines and depends on the criteria used to deﬁne athlete status.11
126	Several studies have also reported associations between speciﬁc genetic polymorphisms
127	and the predisposition to distinct categories of sports-related injuries, such as those affect-
128	ing muscle tissue, bone structure, and concussions, which differ substantially in their
129	underlying pathophysiology.1,12–16 Genetic susceptibility is most often investigated
130	through the analysis of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), the most prevalent
131	form of genetic variation in the human genome. Other types of variants, including inser-
132	tion–deletion polymorphisms, have likewise been implicated in modulating injury risk
133	and recovery, potentially through effects on gene expression or protein function. Each

240	Genetic polymorphisms related to muscle injuries in athletes
241	Muscle injuries result from damage to muscle ﬁbers, caused by, for example, a contusion
242	(sudden impact) or a strain (excessive tensile force). These injuries often lead to myoﬁber rup-
243	ture, typically near the myotendinous junction.24 Common in sports, they can be classiﬁed by
244	mechanism, location, severity, and recurrence frequency.25 Research has shown associations
245	between various genetic variants and susceptibility to muscle injuries in athletes (Table 1),
246	focusing on genes involved in muscle structure, regeneration, energy metabolism, contrac-
247	tion, and the regulation of inﬂammation and oxidative stress response.26,27 This review iden-
248	tiﬁed 17 genes and 21 polymorphisms linked to muscle injuries.

261	elongation of muscle ﬁbers. One signiﬁcant variant is the R577X or C577 T polymorphism
262	(rs1815739) in the ACTN3 gene, where arginine (R) is replaced by a stop codon (X) at position

364	Genes, inﬂammatory response, and muscle repair mechanisms in athletes
365	The inﬂammatory phase is the ﬁrst stage of muscle repair, characterized by the disorgan-
366	ization of myoﬁbrils and vascular ruptures following mechanical or metabolic stress.65
367	This structural disruption leads to the release of pro-inﬂammatory mediators, such as
368	cytokines and chemokines, into the extracellular space. These signals attract immune
369	cells to the site of injury and contribute to the formation of a hematoma.66 This process
370	also activates proteolytic enzymes, stimulates cell proliferation and migration, and initi-
371	ates the repair of damaged cell membranes. In addition, calcium inﬂux triggers several
372	intracellular signaling pathways, such as NF-κB, MAPK, PI3 K/Akt, and JAK/STAT,
373	that facilitate the removal of cellular debris and promote tissue regeneration.67 In this con-
374	text, genetic polymorphisms may inﬂuence the inﬂammatory response and the extent of
375	muscle recovery. For example, the CCR2 gene variants rs768539 and rs3918358 have
376	been associated with reduced pre-exercise strength, impaired strength recovery, and
377	increased pain perception in some individuals.37 Furthermore, no association was found
378	between the rs768539 polymorphism of the CCR2 gene and hamstring injuries in football
379	players.47 CCR2 polymorphisms appear to modulate the intensity of the inﬂammatory
380	response and the efﬁciency of muscle recovery, although their impact on actual injury
381	risk remains uncertain. Similarly, the GG genotype of the CNTF gene (rs2515362) has
382	been associated with better adaptability to strength training, potentially leading to greater
383	muscle gains, improved resistance to injuries, and enhanced fatigue tolerance in sports
384	school students.38 This suggests that CNTF variants may act as modulators of neuromus-
385	cular adaptation, with implications for both performance and resilience to injury. In add-
386	ition, a study conducted among football players revealed a signiﬁcant association
387	between the rs9290271 polymorphism of the LIF gene and muscle injuries and recovery
388	time.43 These ﬁndings indicate that LIF polymorphisms could inﬂuence tissue repair
389	dynamics, potentially serving as markers for predicting recovery duration after muscle
390	injuries. Finally, the T allele of the HGF gene (rs5745678) seems to offer protection
391	against severe injuries, likely by enhancing HGF-mediated muscle regeneration pro-
392	cesses such as activation of muscle stem cells, promotion of anti-inﬂammatory macro-
393	phage phenotypes, and inhibition of ﬁbrosis, which collectively contribute to faster
394	recovery times.68 Furthermore, the CA/AA genotypes (rs5745697) are linked to minor

Abstract
Understanding how genetic and epigenetic factors inﬂuence predisposition, susceptibility,
protection, severity, and recovery potential in sports-related muscle, bone, and brain injuries
is gaining increasing attention, as these injuries represent a major concern for athletes’
health and performance. This narrative review explores the role of speciﬁc genetic variants,
such as those in ACE, ACTN3, AMPD1, VDR, and APOE, in predisposing athletes to injury.
In parallel, the emerging role of microRNAs, including miR-21, miR-133a, miR-208a, and
miR-214 in regulating gene expression related to muscle regeneration, inﬂammation, and
neuroprotection, is highlighted. These small noncoding RNAs are inﬂuenced by environ-
mental stimuli such as sports activity and training, and may serve as promising biomarkers

Introduction
The predisposition to injury and sports performance is primarily determined by intrinsic
biological traits, including genetic polymorphisms that inﬂuence muscle structure, bone
density, and neuromuscular function. While training and other extrinsic factors can
modulate injury risk, they do not deﬁne the baseline predisposition, which is rooted in
these intrinsic characteristics.
    The Healthy Injury-Free Adolescent Athletes study has shown that multiple factors,
including biomechanical, environmental, and psychosocial aspects, contribute signiﬁ-
cantly to injury risk in young athletes.1 Similarly, studies on Olympic athletes have
demonstrated that elite-level performance tends to run in families, emphasizing the
important contribution of genetic background.2 Foundational studies further suggest
that up to 60–70% of the variability in physiological adaptations to physical activity
(such as VO2max and strength gains) and injury susceptibility may be explained by gen-
etic factors.3 Engaging in intense physical activity comes with an increased risk of injur-
ies, the nature and severity of which vary depending on the sport. Indeed, each sport has a
speciﬁc risk proﬁle, related to its unique physical and technical demands. Nearly 70% of
track and ﬁeld athletes experience injuries per season.4 Lower limb injuries are extremely
common in certain sports, affecting 50% of athletes participating in football, marathon,
triathlon, gymnastics (female), basketball, pole vaulting, rugby sevens, volleyball
(female), handball, and tennis.5 Among these injuries, muscular injuries such as ham-
string strains are particularly prevalent; for instance, professional footballers experience
a 20% hamstring injury rate per season, with 20% of these progressing to a chronic stage.6
Stress fractures and stress reactions, while less frequent, pose a greater challenge due to
their longer recovery periods, with athletes requiring on average 67.4 days (± 73.1) to
return to full training for stress reactions, and up to 199 days (± 205.2) for stress frac-
tures.7 In comparison, concussions, though less common, are a growing concern in con-
tact sports, with rugby union players experiencing concussion rates between 8.2 and
16.11 per 1000 h of activity, Gaelic football players 5.21 per 1000 h, and football players
 Marrouh et al.                                                                                  3


between 2.08 and 4.04 per 1000 activity events.8 Beyond the biological and environmen-
tal factors inﬂuencing predisposition and injury risk, it is important to consider the sig-
niﬁcant economic impact of sports injuries. A recent literature review revealed that,
despite methodological heterogeneity, studies consistently report substantial direct and
indirect costs associated with sports injuries, including medical expenses, income loss,
and reduced quality of life.9 For example, a study conducted in Switzerland analyzing
702 injuries in amateur football estimated an average cost of €4030 per injury, with costs
reaching up to €8190 for players over 30 competing in speciﬁc amateur leagues.10 These
ﬁgures illustrate the considerable burden sports injuries place on healthcare systems and
individuals, underscoring the urgent need for effective prevention and management strat-
egies tailored to the speciﬁc demands of each sport.
    Research has increasingly focused on the genetic basis of athletic status. For example,
a genome-wide linkage scan involving 700 pairs of British dizygotic twins estimated that
approximately 66% of the variance in athlete status could be explained by genetic factors,
according to the speciﬁc assumptions of the twin study design. This estimate, however,
varies across sport disciplines and depends on the criteria used to deﬁne athlete status.11
Several studies have also reported associations between speciﬁc genetic polymorphisms
and the predisposition to distinct categories of sports-related injuries, such as those affect-
ing muscle tissue, bone structure, and concussions, which differ substantially in their
underlying pathophysiology.1,12–16 Genetic susceptibility is most often investigated
through the analysis of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), the most prevalent
form of genetic variation in the human genome. Other types of variants, including inser-
tion–deletion polymorphisms, have likewise been implicated in modulating injury risk
and recovery, potentially through effects on gene expression or protein function. Each
SNP may give rise to distinct genotypes, such as homozygous (e.g., AA or TT) or het-
erozygous (e.g., AT) combinations. These genotypes can inﬂuence gene expression or
protein function and are frequently examined to investigate associations with athletic per-
formance, injury risk, or recovery potential.17
    Epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation and microRNAs (miRNAs), modulate
gene activity and are inﬂuenced by exercise and environmental factors. MicroRNAs are a class
of small, noncoding RNA molecules approximately 20–22 nucleotides long that regulate gene
expression at the posttranscriptional level by binding to messenger RNAs and promoting their
degradation or inhibiting their translation. They are key regulators of biological processes,
including tissue repair, inﬂammation, and muscle regeneration, thereby impacting injury sus-
ceptibility and recovery dynamics. In the context of concussions, they are involved in neuroin-
ﬂammatory responses and neuronal repair. Understanding these genetic and epigenetic
contributions enables sports medicine professionals to identify athletes at higher risk of injury,
to personalize training and recovery protocols based on each athlete’s genetic and epigenetic
proﬁle, which may inﬂuence muscle repair capacity, inﬂammatory responses, bone remodel-
ing, and neurological recovery. This could involve aligning training variables, such as inten-
sity, type (e.g., explosive vs. endurance emphasis), volume, and recovery duration, with the
athlete’s speciﬁc biological predispositions. For example, individuals with SNPs or miRNA
expression patterns linked to slower tissue repair or higher inﬂammation might beneﬁt from
more conservative return-to-play timelines, targeted anti-inﬂammatory strategies, longer rest

understanding injury mechanisms. To complement the database search, reference lists of
selected articles were screened manually, and citation tracking was used to identify fur-
ther relevant studies.

Genetic polymorphisms related to muscle injuries in athletes
Muscle injuries result from damage to muscle ﬁbers, caused by, for example, a contusion
(sudden impact) or a strain (excessive tensile force). These injuries often lead to myoﬁber rup-
ture, typically near the myotendinous junction.24 Common in sports, they can be classiﬁed by
mechanism, location, severity, and recurrence frequency.25 Research has shown associations
between various genetic variants and susceptibility to muscle injuries in athletes (Table 1),
focusing on genes involved in muscle structure, regeneration, energy metabolism, contrac-
tion, and the regulation of inﬂammation and oxidative stress response.26,27 This review iden-
tiﬁed 17 genes and 21 polymorphisms linked to muscle injuries.


Genes, muscle structure, and integrity in athletes
Intensive exercise can induce changes in muscle ﬁber structure and organization, which
are inﬂuenced by several genes associated with muscle composition, function, and
 6                                                                       Science Progress 108(4)


particularly muscle contraction. These genetic variants enable athletes to adapt better to
training while resisting muscle injuries. Collagen plays a vital role in regulating collagen ﬁbril
formation and organization in various connective tissues, including skeletal muscle.27 Genetic
variants inﬂuencing muscle structure and integrity are crucial for maintaining the stability and
elongation of muscle ﬁbers. One signiﬁcant variant is the R577X or C577 T polymorphism
(rs1815739) in the ACTN3 gene, where arginine (R) is replaced by a stop codon (X) at position
577. This polymorphism is also referred to using the nucleotide nomenclature, with
R = C and X = T. Individuals with the homozygous XX genotype lack α-actinin-3, making
them more prone to muscle injuries.29 Whereas those with the RR or RX genotypes produce
α-actinin-3, with higher expression in RR individuals.48 According to the literature, results on
ACTN3 are not uniform across studies. Six studies reported no association between the
ACTN3 polymorphism and muscle injuries, particularly in football and rugby
players,16,49–51 as well as in runners and endurance athletes.48,52 However, a larger group
of studies has reported associations between R577X polymorphism of the ACTN3 gene
and an increased predisposition to muscle injuries in football players,26,28,29,33,35,50,53,54
half marathon runners,55 and marathon runners.56 This vulnerability is attributed to increased
instability of the Z discs and, consequently, the sarcomere, resulting in excessive polymeriza-
tion of actin ﬁlaments. This disruption can compromise the effective transmission of muscle
contraction signals and lead to a decrease in the force generated by muscle ﬁbers.53
    Among the studies that found this association, the X allele is associated with an
increased risk of muscle injuries compared to the R allele.28,33,34 Moreover, the XX geno-
type appears linked to longer recovery times35 and lower match performance values than
RR players..53 In contrast, the R allele is signiﬁcantly more prevalent among female
athletes with muscle injuries in sports such as football, softball, basketball, and badmin-
ton (p = 0.04),36 and also in those with injuries related to endurance running training.56
The recent narrative review by Kahya and Taheri, which provides a stratiﬁed synthesis of
genetic markers by sport type and gene function, supports the association of ACTN3
R577X polymorphism with soft-tissue injury risk, particularly in strength- and
endurance-based disciplines.57 Additionally, the R allele of ACTN3 has been shown to
protect football players from developing muscle injuries29 and is linked to a decrease
in serum creatine kinase (CK) levels.55 Pimenta et al. showed that CK levels (4 h after
exercise), cortisol levels (2 h after exercise), and alpha-actin levels (postexercise) were
generally higher in Brazilian professional football players with the ACTN3 XX genotype.
However, the results also showed that the R allele was signiﬁcantly associated with
higher levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6).54 Finally, a marginal association was detected for
ACTN3 rs1815739, where athletes with the R allele seem more likely to experience mus-
cle pain (MP) after exercise than those with the XX genotype.58 A systematic review
found that the XX genotype is associated with sports injuries, particularly among elite
athletes.59 Overall, ACTN3 polymorphisms appear to inﬂuence injury risk through
both structural mechanisms (Z-disc and sarcomere instability) and biochemical pathways
(CK, cortisol, IL-6). These effects are modulated by athlete sex, sport type, and recovery
response. This integrative view reconciles divergent ﬁndings across studies and suggests
that ACTN3 could serve as a practical marker to guide personalized training loads and
recovery strategies.
 Marrouh et al.                                                                                 7


    Several studies have highlighted the role of the MLCK gene in susceptibility to muscle
injuries, with two polymorphisms of the MLCK gene linked to a decrease in postexercise
strength. Heterozygous CA individuals for the c.37885 C > A polymorphism may experi-
ence greater muscle damage after endurance competitions compared to those with the CC
genotype.46 and the frequency of the CA genotype among injured athletes (32.7%) was
not higher than that observed in uninjured athletes (48.9%).52 In contrast, this polymorph-
ism is associated with an increased risk of muscle tears in professional football players,
where the CA genotype is linked to a higher incidence of match injuries, while the CC geno-
type offers protection.16 Furthermore, the GT genotype of the MYLK gene rs28497577 was
associated with prolonged absence due to a knee injury in football players.60 Moreover, poly-
morphisms in the MLCK gene were signiﬁcantly associated with injuries in amateur female
football players, with a different genotypic distribution between injured and uninjured players
(p = 0.031).33 However, CC genotype for the MLCK gene polymorphism c.37885 C > A
exhibited higher serum myoglobin concentrations and greater pre-to-post-race leg muscle
power reduction compared to those with the CA genotype,61 and also the AA genotype
was found to be advantageous for increasing body mass index (BMI) after creatine supple-
mentation compared to the CA and CC genotypes.49 These ﬁndings suggest that the impact of
MLCK variants is context-dependent: in some cases (e.g., football players), the CA genotype
increases injury susceptibility, while in others (e.g., endurance runners), it is associated with
lower risk but greater postexercise muscle damage. This dual role highlights the importance
of sport-speciﬁc demands and recovery dynamics and suggests that MLCK polymorphisms
could guide personalized strengthening programs and postexercise monitoring.
    In soccer players, research has shown that the GA genotype (c.*800A > G) of the CKM
gene had a higher frequency of musculoskeletal injuries and increased injury severity dur-
ing the season. Furthermore, players with the GG genotype have a higher incidence of
injuries during training compared to matches.16 The GG genotype had a higher frequency
in training injuries compared to those observed in matches (p = 0.038).33 Additionally, in
athletes, the frequency of the A allele is signiﬁcantly higher among those who have sus-
tained injuries (47.3%) compared to those who have not (42.2%).52 Players with the GG
genotype (c.*800A > G) also demonstrate an increased response in terms of muscle mass
and BMI during creatine supplementation, highlighting the importance of this genotype
in the performance of power athletes.49 Overall, CKM polymorphisms appear to inﬂuence
both injury risk and recovery potential, while also modulating responses to supplemen-
tation, suggesting their value as markers for adjusting training load and optimizing per-
formance in strength-oriented disciplines. Furthermore, the rs1800255 polymorphism of
the COL3A1 gene has been examined in two studies has examined the rs1800255 poly-
morphism of the COL3A1 gene in relation to muscle injuries in athletes. The ﬁrst study
found an association between the A allele of this polymorphism and rugby athlete status
and increased resistance to soft tissue injuries.39 In contrast, the second study found no cor-
relation between this polymorphism and exercise-induced muscle cramps.62 Although ﬁnd-
ings remain inconsistent, evidence suggests that COL3A1 variants may inﬂuence soft tissue
resilience, which could be considered in training planning and injury prevention strategies.
Indeed, the rs12722 polymorphism of the COL5A1 gene is associated with muscle injuries
in elite Australian Football League players.40 Additionally, the C allele of COL5A1 has
 8                                                                      Science Progress 108(4)


been associated with a reduced risk of muscle injuries in Italian football players.29 Similarly,
another study revealed that COL5A1 rs12722 accounted for 44% of injury severity
(p = 0.002).41 These results are consistent with those of Heffernan et al., who reported a sig-
niﬁcant association between the inferred C-C allele combination, meaning the simultaneous
presence of the C allele at both the rs12722 and rs3196378 polymorphic sites, and protection
against muscle injuries.27 Similarly, O’Connell et al., found that the CC genotype was
associated with protection against exercise-associated muscle cramping.62 However,
two other studies found no association between the different rs12722 genotypes and mus-
cle injury risk.63,64 However, other studies failed to detect associations between rs12722
genotypes and injury risk.63,64 These discrepancies suggest that COL5A1 may inﬂuence
injury susceptibility in a sport- or context-dependent manner.


Genes, inﬂammatory response, and muscle repair mechanisms in athletes
The inﬂammatory phase is the ﬁrst stage of muscle repair, characterized by the disorgan-
ization of myoﬁbrils and vascular ruptures following mechanical or metabolic stress.65
This structural disruption leads to the release of pro-inﬂammatory mediators, such as
cytokines and chemokines, into the extracellular space. These signals attract immune
cells to the site of injury and contribute to the formation of a hematoma.66 This process
also activates proteolytic enzymes, stimulates cell proliferation and migration, and initi-
ates the repair of damaged cell membranes. In addition, calcium inﬂux triggers several
intracellular signaling pathways, such as NF-κB, MAPK, PI3 K/Akt, and JAK/STAT,
that facilitate the removal of cellular debris and promote tissue regeneration.67 In this con-
text, genetic polymorphisms may inﬂuence the inﬂammatory response and the extent of
muscle recovery. For example, the CCR2 gene variants rs768539 and rs3918358 have
been associated with reduced pre-exercise strength, impaired strength recovery, and
increased pain perception in some individuals.37 Furthermore, no association was found
between the rs768539 polymorphism of the CCR2 gene and hamstring injuries in football
players.47 CCR2 polymorphisms appear to modulate the intensity of the inﬂammatory
response and the efﬁciency of muscle recovery, although their impact on actual injury
risk remains uncertain. Similarly, the GG genotype of the CNTF gene (rs2515362) has
been associated with better adaptability to strength training, potentially leading to greater
muscle gains, improved resistance to injuries, and enhanced fatigue tolerance in sports
school students.38 This suggests that CNTF variants may act as modulators of neuromus-
cular adaptation, with implications for both performance and resilience to injury. In add-
ition, a study conducted among football players revealed a signiﬁcant association
between the rs9290271 polymorphism of the LIF gene and muscle injuries and recovery
time.43 These ﬁndings indicate that LIF polymorphisms could inﬂuence tissue repair
dynamics, potentially serving as markers for predicting recovery duration after muscle
injuries. Finally, the T allele of the HGF gene (rs5745678) seems to offer protection
against severe injuries, likely by enhancing HGF-mediated muscle regeneration pro-
cesses such as activation of muscle stem cells, promotion of anti-inﬂammatory macro-
phage phenotypes, and inhibition of ﬁbrosis, which collectively contribute to faster
recovery times.68 Furthermore, the CA/AA genotypes (rs5745697) are linked to minor
 Marrouh et al.                                                                               9


injuries and also promote faster recovery in football players.43 Overall, HGF polymorph-
isms appear to support regenerative capacity and recovery quality, reinforcing their
potential importance in injury prevention strategies.

403	Genes and muscle energy metabolism in athletes
404	Energetic regulation plays an important role in maintaining cellular energy homeostasis,
405	thus ensuring better muscle contraction function and movement. The accumulation of
406	waste products can damage cells and make them more susceptible to injuries during high-
407	intensity activities, which is particularly noticeable in certain athletes. This is due to dis-
408	ruptions caused by genetic variants that affect energy metabolism, as well as oxidative
409	stress related to waste accumulation and a decrease in the transport of metabolites and
410	energy substrates.15,16,33 The polymorphism c.34C > T (rs17602729) of the AMPD1
411	gene has been extensively studied in the context of sports injuries. Research has shown
412	that individuals carrying the T allele, especially those with the TT genotype, are more
413	likely to develop metabolic myopathies characterized by exercise-induced muscle symp-
414	toms such as early fatigue, cramps, and myalgias. These symptoms increase their injury
415	risk, particularly in demanding sports like football.15,16,33 Furthermore, athletes with the
416	TT genotype exhibit decreased exercise capacity and cardiorespiratory responses, as well
417	as a limited response to endurance training, which may also contribute to an increased
418	risk of injury. Studies indicate that football players with the CC genotype of the
419	AMPD1 gene experience fewer ankle and knee injuries and play more matches than those
420	expressing a T allele. This is true for both professional and amateur football players, sug-
421	gesting that the CC genotype may offer protection against injuries.15,16,33 This link
422	between the AMPD1 polymorphism and sports injuries is particularly relevant for endur-
423	ance athletes, where optimal muscle metabolism is essential for injury prevention.52
424	Overall, AMPD1 polymorphisms appear to shape individual susceptibility to muscle
425	injuries by inﬂuencing energy metabolism efﬁciency and tolerance to high physical
426	demands. Moreover, the AA genotype of the gene MCT1 (rs1049434) is associated
427	with a signiﬁcant increase in muscle injuries in elite football players compared to the
428	TT genotype.44 Furthermore, Italian football players with the TT genotype have a signiﬁ-
429	cantly higher percentage of lean body mass than those with the AA genotype, suggesting
430	that the T allele is linked to better body composition in young athletes.45 Additionally,
431	another study conducted on Italian football players revealed that carriers of the T allele
432	have a protective effect against muscle injuries.29 One study reported a transmission dis-
433	tortion, meaning in this case a deviation from the Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium at the
434	population level, of the MCT1 rs1049434 polymorphism, with an overrepresentation of
435	the T allele among elite Polish athletes, including both endurance athletes (3000 m, mara-
436	thon, cross-country skiing, swimming, triathlon, and rowing) and power/speed athletes
437	(100–400 m sprint, weightlifting, and powerlifting).69 However, no signiﬁcant difference
438	was observed in the allele distribution of the A/T polymorphism (rs1049434) of the
439	MCT1 gene between athletes and the control group, suggesting that this polymorphism
440	may not inﬂuence muscle injury susceptibility in young athletes preparing for the
441	Turkish Youth Championship.70 Taken together, MCT1 polymorphisms may contribute

446	ﬁndings remain population- and sport-speciﬁc.

449	Genes, cardiovascular, and muscle regulation in athletes
450	Cardiovascular and muscular regulation is essential for maintaining muscle integrity by
451	regulating oxygen supply and blood transport through arteries and veins. Genetic variants
452	have been associated with vasodilation issues, which can lead to a decrease in blood pres-
453	sure. The imbalance in this regulation causes muscle fatigue and the accumulation of
454	metabolic waste. This makes muscles more susceptible to injuries, especially during
455	training. Genetic variants play a key role in cardiovascular and muscular regulation.71,72
456	For example, motor activity induces dynamic changes in ACE gene expression in rats,
457	with bioinformatics analysis linking these shifts to cardiovascular regulation and electro-
458	lyte balance during endurance exercise.73 A common genetic variation known as the ACE
459	I/D polymorphism (rs1799752) alters the expression of the ACE enzyme and may affect
460	cardiovascular health. This polymorphism results from the insertion (I) or deletion (D) of
461	a 287 bp Alu sequence within intron 16 of the ACE gene, resulting in three distinct gen-
462	otypes: II, ID, and DD.74 Increased activity of the ACE enzyme, often associated with the
463	D allele, promotes the production of angiotensin II while decreasing the half-life of
464	bradykinin. This dynamic may inﬂuence inﬂammatory responses following muscle
465	injury, given that angiotensin II and bradykinin play signiﬁcant roles in inﬂammation.75
466	Sierra et al. have suggested a link between ACE I/D gene polymorphisms and suscepti-
467	bility to postexercise muscle injuries, particularly sport-related muscle damage (SRMD).
468	These polymorphisms could inﬂuence sensitivity to such damage by modulating the
469	inﬂammatory response.30 According to research, several studies have highlighted the
470	association of the D allele of the ACE I/D polymorphism with a lower risk of muscle
471	injuries and its protective role against these injuries.29–31 Other studies have reported a
472	correlation between the D allele and lower CK levels,32 a marker of muscle damage, fol-
473	lowing intense efforts such as triathlons55 and marathons.30 Conversely, another study
474	found that athletes with the ID genotype had a higher incidence of sports injuries com-
475	pared to those with the DD and II genotypes.76 Moreover, an interaction between poly-
476	morphisms was observed: the combination of the X allele of the ACTN3 gene with the II
477	genotype of ACE I/D resulted in a twofold increase in injury incidence per season.28
478	Other studies found no association between the ACE I/D polymorphism and muscle injur-
479	ies.16,33,47,49,51,52 Overall, these ﬁndings highlight the complexity of ACE polymorphism
480	effects, which may depend on genotype interactions, type of sport, and study population.
481	Furthermore, the G allele of the NOS3 gene (1799983) appears to have reduced sensitiv-
482	ity to proteolytic cleavage, which may promote increased enzyme activity and, conse-
483	quently, enhanced production of NOS3.77 To date, only two studies have investigated
484	the association between NOS3 gene polymorphisms and injuries in athletes. One study

487	another study in high-level Brazilian athletes did not ﬁnd any signiﬁcant association
488	between the rs1799983 polymorphism of the NOS3 gene and MP or traumatic muscle

497	Genes and hormonal regulation of muscle in athletes
498	Hormonal regulation, including estrogen, is crucial for stress response and muscle func-
499	tion. Imbalances can impair muscle function, increasing injury risk in athletes.
500	Polymorphisms in the ESR1 gene (rs2234693 C/T, rs9340799 G/A) affect receptor
501	expression and estrogen action. The C allele of rs2234693 may protect against muscle
502	injuries by reducing muscle stiffness.42 Overall, ESR1 variants may inﬂuence susceptibil-
503	ity to muscle injuries by affecting hormonal regulation of muscle tone and recovery.

513	ive tissue remodeling, like the NOGGIN gene, are crucial for maintaining balance.
514	A study found a higher incidence of muscle injuries in carriers of the GG genotype
515	(rs1372857), who was more likely to suffer moderate to severe injuries in elite
516	Australian football players.40 Variants regulating muscle growth, cytoskeletal dynamics,
517	and connective tissue remodeling collectively contribute to individual differences in
518	injury risk and recovery potential.
